title: Everything we knew about software has changed: think wider, not just bigger
summary: Theo argues that each model era (tool calls, long-running tasks, orchestration) shifts what one builder can ship, so old project tiers have dropped a level. Devs must drop skeuomorphic habits and sunk-cost attachments, then build wider across a product's breadth instead of only deeper.

principles.text: Models improve faster than we do, so the move is to build bigger, not to get better at the same work.
principles.quote: The models are getting better faster than we are. So, we can't necessarily get better. So, instead we have to go bigger.

principles.text: Prompt the model to orchestrate and verify; you don't need custom tooling or a software factory to go further.
principles.quote: You don't need some custom tooling, some custom system, some fancy software factory. You just need to prompt it to go a little further.

principles.text: Question habits that exist only because "it's how we've always done it": identity tied to languages, sunk-cost code, guilt merges.
principles.quote: Is this how we do things cuz it's right, or is this how we do things cuz it's just how we've always done it?

principles.text: Project tiers have shifted down one level: yesterday's startup is today's side project, and some products are now just a markdown file on a cron.
principles.quote: Now that the models are bigger, the tiers have shifted. Everything is now one tier lower.

principles.text: Think wider: cover broad range across a category, and let users build missing depth themselves if you architect the product to be extensible.
principles.quote: If you architect your systems and you architect your products in such a way that users can do things that they you never would have guessed.

principles.text: If your idea doesn't feel stupidly ambitious, it isn't big enough.
principles.quote: If your idea doesn't feel stupid, it's cuz your idea's not big enough.
